Bill measurements are one of the classic ways to tell penguin species apart.
Here I check how well bill length and depth separate them, using Python.

Data: [Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/),
Palmer Station Antarctica LTER (CC0 licence). Loaded from the `palmerpenguins`
Python package.

## Loading and tidying

```{python}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()
bills = penguins.dropna(subset=["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"])

print(len(penguins), "penguins,", len(bills), "with complete bill measurements")
```

## Summary by species

```{python}
bills.groupby("species")[["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]].mean().round(1)
```

Adelie penguins have the shortest bills, Chinstrap the longest, and Gentoo
bills are noticeably shallower than the other two.

## Bill length versus depth

```{python}
#| label: fig-bill-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Bill length versus bill depth, coloured by species."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for species, group in bills.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(group["bill_length_mm"], group["bill_depth_mm"],
               label=species, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Bill depth (mm)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()
```

@fig-bill-scatter shows three fairly distinct clusters. Overall the trend
between length and depth looks negative, but that is an illusion of pooling:
within each species the relationship is positive.

```{python}
bills.groupby("species").apply(
    lambda g: g["bill_length_mm"].corr(g["bill_depth_mm"]),
    include_groups=False,
).round(2)
```

This is Simpson's paradox in a small, friendly form: the pooled correlation and
the within-species correlations have opposite signs.
